readingSections.title: Arrays and Strings: indexing, contiguous storage, two-pointer and sliding window
readingSections.quickSummary: Array contiguous fixed-type storage plus O(1) random access via index plus O(n) insert or delete in the middle. String is array of chars plus often immutable. Two pointers scan from opposite ends. Sliding window keeps a variable-length interval that grows and shrinks.
content: An array is a contiguous block where every element has the same size and type so address equals base plus index times element size. That single fact gives O(1) random access: arr[5] is direct math, not a search. Cost appears elsewhere: inserting or deleting in the middle needs shifting — worst O(n) moves — and resizing beyond capacity may allocate a new block plus copy all. The exam loves array vs linked list where array wins on random access but linked list wins on insertion without shifting.

A string is an array of characters with language flavour: in Java and Python strings are immutable (every so-called change builds a new string plus hides O(n) copy cost), in C they are mutable arrays terminated by null, in JavaScript they are UTF-16 sequences with surrogate pairs. String operations the exam rotates: length, concatenation, substring via slice, compare lexicographically, reverse, and pattern search via built-ins or two-pointer scan.

Two-pointer is the pattern that saves marks on arrays and strings. Place one pointer at the start and one at the end and move inward based on a condition. Palindrome check increments left while decrementing right; sorted two-sum moves low plus high towards the target from both ends; removing duplicates from a sorted array keeps a write pointer and a read pointer. The exam draws an array with two arrows and asks number of comparisons — count pointer moves.

Sliding window keeps a window [left, right] that grows by moving right and shrinks by moving left while an invariant holds (distinct characters, sum less than K, exactly K distinct). Window carets keep maximum or minimum plus window length and best seen. Typical questions: longest substring without repeating characters, smallest subarray covering a target, count with at most K distinct. The exam swaps the words at most vs exactly and the fix is subtracting one count from the other.

Array primitives to have ready: prefix sums let range sum queries be O(1) after O(n) build via prefix[i] equals sum up to i; sparse arrays waste space (bitmap or map may compress); sorted arrays enable binary search; sparse plus two-pointer plus prefix sum maps directly to substring vs subarray stems.

subsections.title: Random access vs insertion plus resize
subsections.content: Random access O(1) via index math is the array headline. Insertion middle O(n) shifts, deletion middle O(n) shifts, append amortized O(1) with occasional resize copy, full resize O(n) allocate plus copy. That table vs linked list O(n) random vs O(1) insert via splice is the mark.

subsections.title: Immutable strings hide copies
subsections.content: On an immutable string each plus or push or slice that logically edits builds a new buffer and copies characters. Repeating plus in a loop yields O(n squared) via repeated copying — prefer a builder such as StringBuilder or list plus join. AXIS commonly writes repeated string concatenation in a loop and asks complexity.

quickRevision: Array contiguous plus O(1) index via base plus index times size; insert/delete middle O(n) shifts; append amortized O(1) via resize copy.
String char array flavour: Java/Python immutable (new string per edit), C mutable, JS UTF-16. Substring via slice, compare lex order, reverse via two pointers.
Two pointers start plus end move inward: palindrome, sorted two-sum, dedup on sorted via write plus read.
Sliding window [left,right] grows right shrinks left per invariant; at most K vs exactly K vs longest with no repeat is the invariant.
Prefix sums range sum O(1) after O(n) build; sparse vs sorted vs string plus immutable nuance vs prefix.
tricks: Any answer that says array insert in the middle is O(1) is wrong — middle insertion is O(n) shifts plus perhaps resize.
Do not swap two-pointer with sliding window — two pointers start at opposite ends and meet; window starts narrow and grows plus shrinks inside.
Immutable strings make repeated plus O(n squared) — builder collect then join is linear.
patterns: 'Contiguous O(1) index vs O(n) insert middle?' -> Array via base plus index, linked list via O(n) walk vs O(1) splice.
'Immutable string repeated concatenation in loop?' -> StringBuilder or list plus join to stay O(n).
'Two arrows from ends inward?' -> Two-pointer. 'Variable [left,right] growing and shrinking vs invariant?' -> Sliding window.
'Range sum query?' -> Prefix sums; sorted two-sum needs array sorted then two pointers.

pyqPatterns.question: Array indexing plus string immutability plus two-pointer vs sliding window plus prefix?
pyqPatterns.approach: Index O(1) math, immutable copies O(n), two pointers meet, window grows plus shrinks, prefix O(1) range sums.

pyqPatterns.question: Palindrome via two pointers vs dedup via write plus read vs two-sum on sorted via opposite ends?
pyqPatterns.approach: Palindromes compare ends inward, dedup sorted keeps write plus read, sorted two-sum opposite ends moving towards target.

readingSections.title: Stacks and Queues: LIFO vs FIFO plus monotonic plus queues for BFS
readingSections.quickSummary: Stack LIFO via push plus pop plus peek (top). Queue FIFO via enqueue plus dequeue plus front. Stacks drive DFS and undo and bracket checks; queues drive BFS and scheduling. Monotonic stack keeps increasing or decreasing to solve next greater or histogram; circular queue via bounded array vs linked queue unbounded.
content: Stack is Last-In First-Out. Only the top is visible. Operations are push on top, pop from top, peek that reads without removing, plus emptiness plus size. Implementation via array needs capacity plus grows via resizing; via linked list links each push. The exam writes expression evaluation steps sequence as stack content after each token — the stack snapshot after each symbol is the mark.

Queue is First-In First-Out. Operations are enqueue at rear, dequeue at front, front or peek that reads front, plus emptiness plus size. Implementation via linked list links each enqueue; via circular array wraps rear to front with head pointer plus tail plus size plus modulo arithmetic. Circular fixes wasted space where plain array leaves bubbles. The exam's circular queue empty vs full via head equals tail test is the classic trap — one slot wasted or size flag breaks the tie.

Applications decide which to pick. Stack drives Depth-First traversal (explicit stack versus recursion's implicit call stack), expression conversion (infix to postfix plus evaluation), balanced parentheses via pushing opens and popping on closes, undo and backtracking. Queue drives Breadth-First traversal (level order), print queue, round-robin buffers, and sliding-window buffering within the array topic.

Monotonic stack is the power-ups the exam loves. An increasing stack on input 2,1,2,4,3 pushes while the stack top is bigger than the next — popping collects next greater elements; a decreasing stack collects next smaller. Next Greater Element to the right is the template: maintain decreasing stack of candidates, pop while top small than incoming, then map popped to incoming as its next greater. Histogram maximum rectangle plus trapped rain water reuse the same structure plus indices plus width.

Two queues can simulate a stack by moving all but the last between queues, and two stacks can simulate a queue by pouring one stack into the other to reverse order. AXIS rarely asks to run the full simulation but writes two queues make a stack or cost analysis for amortized time — amortized O(1) via each element moved at most twice is the expected phrasing.

subsections.title: Stack snapshot of expression evaluation
subsections.content: Postfix evaluation scans left to right: push numbers, on operator pop two, apply, push result. Tracing the stack contents after each token is a frequent one-mark diagram — count depth matches operand vs operator balance.

subsections.title: Circular queue tie-break that steals marks
subsections.content: On a bounded array head tracks dequeue, tail tracks enqueue, size tracks occupancy. Head equals tail means both empty plus full — so keep one empty slot or a count. That one empty slot is the baked-in waste that many stems forget to mention.

quickRevision: Stack LIFO push plus pop plus peek top via array plus resize or linked; queue FIFO enqueue at rear plus dequeue at front via circular array plus modulo or linked.
Stack drives DFS plus expressions plus undo plus brackets; queue drives BFS plus scheduling plus buffering.
Monotonic increasing vs decreasing stack for next greater or smaller plus histogram via indices.
Circular queue head plus tail plus size plus one wasted slot or flag separates empty vs full.
Two stacks simulate queue and two queues simulate stack via reversals — amortized O(1) each element at most twice.
tricks: Any answer that says queue uses LIFO is swapping — LIFO is stack, FIFO is queue.
Do not attach BFS to stack — BFS uses queue for level order, DFS uses stack plus recursion for depth.
Circular empty equals full tie-break requires one wasted slot or size flag — any answer that says head equals tail alone decides without tie-breaker is wrong for bounded circular.
patterns: 'Last pushed first popped?' -> Stack. 'First enqueued first dequeued?' -> Queue.
'Expression evaluation stack trace plus balanced parentheses?' -> Stack push opens pop on closes.
'Level order vs depth?' -> Queue for BFS vs stack or recursion for DFS.
'Next greater or histogram plus trapped rain?' -> Monotonic stack with indices.
'Queue on a bounded array wraps?' -> Circular plus head plus tail plus size.

pyqPatterns.approach: LIFO top vs FIFO front; stack recursion depth, queue levels; parentheses push opens pop closes check emptiness and matching type.

pyqPatterns.question: Next Greater via decreasing stack vs trapped rain or histogram via stack plus circular equality plus two Stacks as queue?
pyqPatterns.approach: Decreasing stack for next greater with popped to incoming map; histogram width times pop; head equals tail needs size or waste flag; pour stack to reverse for queue simulation.

readingSections.title: Trees and Graphs: traversals plus BST plus heaps vs trie plus BFS vs DFS plus representation
readingSections.quickSummary: Tree acyclic connected with one path between any two nodes, rooted gives parent plus child plus height plus depth. Binary tree max two children; BST left smaller right larger plus ordered. Traversals: inorder sorted on BST, preorder, postorder, level BFS via queue. Heap complete array with heapify O(n). Trie prefix tree as nested array plus bit vector. Graph nodes plus edges with adjacency list vs matrix trade-off. BFS queue shortest on unweighted, DFS stack/recursion for connectivity plus cycle plus topo via stack.
content: A tree is an acyclic connected graph with one unique path between any two nodes. A rooted tree fixes a root and imposes direction: parent, children, siblings, leaf with no child, height as longest root-to-leaf edge count (often counted as node count differs by one; pick leaf height 0 vs 1 as per stem), depth as root-to-node edges. Binary tree restricts each node to at most two children — left and right matter for ordered trees. Balanced plus AVL vs red-black rarely need rotation tracing on AXIS beyond awareness.

BST (Binary Search Tree) adds order: left subtree holds keys smaller than node, right holds larger, duplicates policy decides side or forbids. Sorted order via inorder traversal is the BST giveaway: inorder on a BST is ascending. Traversals by type: inorder for BST sorted (left+node+right), preorder for copy and prefix ops (node+left+right), postorder for delete and postfix (left+right+node), level order plus BFS via queue for width first. The exam writes such bursts as traversal strings plus asks which BST would produce this preorder or which stack vs queue matches which traversal.

Heap is the array-backed complete binary tree that respects the heap property: min-heap parent smaller than children, max-heap parent larger. Index via parent i, children 2*i plus 1/2 for 0-based. Build in O(n) via linear heapify from the last non-leaf downwards, not N inserts. Priority queue is the abstraction; heap is the implementation. Trie (prefix tree) stores strings as a tree of characters sharing prefixes; bit vector plus nested arrays plus terminal flag compress sequential lookups — lookup remains O(L) where L is key length.

Graphs are networks: node (vertex) plus edges weighted or unweighted, directed or undirected, possibly with cycles. Representation splits. Adjacency matrix is n times n grid of 0/1 or weights plus dense but O(n squared) space plus O(1) edge existence; adjacency list is array of per-vertex neighbor lists plus sparse-friendly O(V plus E) plus average neighbour enumeration fast but edge existence linear. The exam word dense vs sparse tells you which representation to quote.

Traversals plus search on graphs. BFS via queue explores level by level and returns the shortest path length on an unweighted graph (distance in edges). DFS via stack or recursion explores depth and helps connectivity plus cycle detection before blackening and topological sort after. Weighted shortest needs Dijkstra after BFS, but AXIS focuses BFS vs DFS vs adjacency as the graph core. Cycle plus bipartite plus connected components also reduce to BFS or DFS colouring — undirected cycle appears as a back edge to a visited not parent.

Why the exam stresses the split: arrays plus strings focus on two-pointer plus window plus prefix; stacks plus queues focus on LIFO vs FIFO plus BFS vs DFS; trees plus graphs focus on traversal plus BST vs heap vs trie vs adjacency plus BFS vs DFS0.

subsections.title: Traversals on BST in one string
subsections.content: Preorder copies and prints prefix: node left right. Inorder sorts BST: left node right. Postorder deletes and prints postfix: left right node. Level traverses by breadth via queue. That four-in-one table saves many marks.

subsections.title: Heap build O(n) vs N inserts O(n log n)
subsections.content: Linear heapify inserts cost O(log n) so N inserts cost N log N; heapify from bottom gives O(n) by skipping leaves. AXIS commonly wants the O(n) heapify claim as the cost to convert an array already random to a heap.

quickRevision: Tree acyclic connected one path plus rooted terms via parent plus children plus leaf plus height vs depth plus binary two children.
BST left smaller right larger plus ordered duplicates policy decides; inorder sorted ascending on BST; preorder node left right vs postorder left right node vs level via queue.
Heap complete array via heapify O(n) vs wrong O(n log n) if built via inserts; min vs max property via parent at i vs children at 2*i plus 1/2 (0-based); priority queue abstraction.
Trie prefix tree as nested arrays via terminal flag plus bit vector; graph adjacency list O(V+E) sparse vs matrix O(n^2) dense via BFS shortest on unweighted vs DFS depth via stack or recursion.
BFS queue shortest plus DFS stack/recursion for connectivity plus cycle plus topo plus representation dense vs sparse. Binary tree shape plus balanced vs AVL vs red-black awareness.
tricks: Any answer that says heap build via N inserts is O(n) is wrong — inserts O(n log n) vs heapify O(n).
Do not attach BFS shortest to weighted graphs — BFS shortest holds only for unweighted; weighted shortest needs Dijkstra.
Inorder always sorted is only true for BST — general binary tree inorder is not sorted.
patterns: 'Left smaller right larger?' -> BST plus inorder sorted via BST.
'Build heap from arbitrary array?' -> Heapify O(n) not N inserts.
'Shortest on unweighted graph plus level order?' -> BFS via queue; 'Depth plus connectivity plus topo?' -> DFS via stack or recursion.
'Adjacency dense vs sparse?' -> Matrix O(n^2) vs list O(V+E).
'Prefix tree via shared prefixes?' -> Trie O(L) on key length.

pyqPatterns.approach: Inorder sorts BST; heap via heapify O(n); trie prefix O(L); adjacency vs matrix by dense vs sparse; BFS queue shortest vs DFS depth.

readingSections.title: Sorting and Searching: bubble vs selection vs insertion vs merge vs quick vs heap plus linear vs binary
readingSections.quickSummary: Sorting orders; complexity vs stability decide. Simple sorts O(n^2): bubble swaps adjacent, selection picks min, insertion like cards shifts. Efficient O(n log n): merge divide conquer stable, quick partition average O(n log n) worst O(n^2) depending on pivot, heap via heapify. Searching: linear O(n) scans all, binary O(log n) needs sorted via dividing mid.
content: Sorting orders keys. Simple O(n squared) sorts: bubble repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order passes and short-circuits if a pass had no swap; selection each pass picks the minimum among unsorted and swaps into place plus smallest writes; insertion walks like playing cards: each new element shifted left into the sorted prefix. Insertion wins for small or nearly sorted on comparisons and moves plus stable with tiny overhead.

Efficient O(n log n) sorts: merge splits in half recursively then merges two sorted halves with a temp buffer — stable and divide plus conquer with O(n) extra plus not in-place but always n log n. Quick picks a pivot plus partitions smaller vs larger via two pointers then recurses on partitions — average n log n, worst n squared when pivot always worst (already sorted plus bad pivot pick); randomized pivot or median-of-three tames it. Heap builds a heap then repeatedly extracts the root.

Stability matters when secondary order must be preserved. Stable sorts keep equal keys in input order: merge plus insertion plus bubble (swapping only adjacent out-of-order strictly stable) plus counting vs radix. Unstable sorts can flip equal keys: selection plus quick (partition moves) plus heap (sifting) are classically unstable but selection can be made stable with extra moves. The exam writes stable vs worst plus average plus in-place as a comparison table.

Searching: linear search walks one by one O(n) without sorting. Binary search needs a sorted array and halves the interval via mid each probe: while left less than equal to right compare mid and narrow, O(log n) comparisons plus O(1) extra; mid update left equals mid plus 1 vs right equals mid minus 1 plus inclusive bounds are the off-by-one traps. The exam's step count on binary search is number of mids probed.

Two counting sources on analysis: swaps vs comparisons vs moves vs recursion depth plus space. Stable plus worst vs space determines which to quote. Counting sort plus radix non-comparison sort count fast for small key ranges (counting O(n plus k) via frequency after stabilization and radix O(d times (n plus k))). AXIS rarely asks to run radix beyond awareness but recognizes non-comparison plus O(n log n) barrier for comparison sorts.

subsections.title: One comparison table that ends the trap
subsections.content: Bubble O(n^2) stable in-place average vs worst quadratic. Selection O(n^2) unstable in-place via picks. Insertion O(n^2) but O(n) on nearly sorted, stable, in-place. Merge O(n log n) stable not in-place with O(n) extra plus always n log n. Quick average O(n log n) unstable in-place plus worst n^2 with very bad pivot. Heap O(n log n) unstable in-place via heapify plus extract. Linear search O(n), binary O(log n) sorted.

subsections.title: Stability check that saves a mark
subsections.content: Swapping only adjacent out-of-order preserves order of equals, hence bubble plus insertion are stable; moving via jumps (selection plus quick plus heap) can leap and flip equals, hence unstable classically.

quickRevision: Simple O(n^2): bubble adjacent swap plus short-circuit, selection pick min swap, insertion like cards shift in — insertion good on nearly sorted and stable.
Efficient O(n log n): merge divide conjoin stable, quick pivot partition average good worst quadratic, heap heapify plus extract — all efficient plus in-place except merge extra.
Stability: stable keeps equals original order: merge plus insertion plus bubble vs unstable: selection plus quick plus heap.
Linear O(n) without sorted vs binary O(log n) needs sorted via mid halving plus inclusive bounds.
Non-comparison counting vs radix bypass comparison lower bound for small key ranges plus non-comparison special case.
tricks: Any answer that says quick is always O(n log n) worst is wrong — pivot choice decides; worst is O(n^2) with consistently bad pivot, average randomized much lower.
Do not swap insertion vs selection inside: insertion shifts, selection picks.
Any answer that says binary search works unsorted is wrong — sorting is mandatory first or linear remains O(n).
patterns: 'Adjacent swaps plus short-circuit if no swap?' -> Bubble O(n^2) stable.
'Picks minimum each pass vs shifts like cards?' -> Selection picks vs insertion shifts. 'Divide plus conquer with temp?' -> Merge stable O(n log n).
'Pivot plus partition plus average vs worst?' -> Quick average n log n worst n^2.
'Needs sorted half via mid?' -> Binary O(log n). 'Scans one by one?' -> Linear O(n).
'Keeps equals order?' -> Stable: merge plus insertion plus bubble; unstable: selection plus quick plus heap.

pyqPatterns.approach: Simple O(n^2) vs efficient O(n log n) plus stable list via adjacent-preserving sorts, binary needs sorted via mid halving.

pyqPatterns.approach: Binary O(log n) mids; quick pivot decides worst; stable bubble via insertion via merge; merge extra space vs quick in-place.

readingSections.title: Complexity (Big-O): asymptotic growth plus best vs average vs worst plus space plus divide plus conquer
readingSections.quickSummary: Big-O upper bound and Omega lower and Theta tight; growth chart tied around constant~1 vs log vs sqrt vs linear vs linearithmic n log n vs quadratic vs cubic vs exponential 2^n vs factorial n!. O counts steps ignoring constants plus lower terms after grouping per faster still dominates slower: n^2 plus n is still n^2. Best vs average vs worst vary by input; space vs time trade-offs, recursion depth vs iterative; Master for divide plus conquer relates cost plus fanout vs combine.
content: Asymptotic means large n. Big-O is upper bound: grows at most as fast as g(n). Omega is lower bound. Theta is tight both. AXIS asks big-O almost exclusively, sometimes big-Theta plus little-o vs little-O. Fudge: ignore constants and lower-order terms — an algorithm of 5 n squared plus 30 n plus 10 is still Theta(n squared) plus O(n squared) plus also O(n cubed) loosely; bound is monotonic after some n0.

Growth ladder that decides in 5 seconds: constant O(1) < log n (binary search) < sqrt(n) < n (linear scan) < n log n (efficient sorts) < n squared (simple sorts) < n cubed (cubic) < 2^n (exponential) < n! (factorial). For fixed n = 1000, log ~10, sqrt ~32, linear 1k, n log n ~10k, n squared 1M, exponential 2^1000 absurd — that absurdity is the exponential vs polynomial split that breaks test cases.

Best vs average vs worst depend on input. Linear search best O(1) when target first, average O(n), worst O(n) when last or missing. Bubble sort best O(n) via sorted plus no swap short-circuit, average plus worst O(n squared). Binary search best O(1) via mid immediate, worst O(log n). Quick best ~O(n log n) via balanced pivot, worst O(n squared) via worst pivot; random pivot fixes average ~n log n. The exam word best plus average plus worst is never filler.

Space plus time plus recursion depth trade: extra space O(1) in-place vs O(n) per buffer such as merge temp vs O(log n) recursion stack for binary search via recursion plus quick plus merge depth. Divide-and-conquer Master theorem for recurrences of the form T(n) = a T(n/b) plus O(n^d) compares a vs b^d: if a less than b^d then leaves dominate => O(n^d); if a equals b^d then balanced => O(n^d log n); if a greater than b^d then children dominate => O(n^{log(b) a}). For merge sort T(n)=2T(n/2) plus O(n) gives a=2, b=2, d=1, b^d=2 so a equals b^d => O(n log n).

Two small facts that steal marks. One, amortized analysis via potential for dynamic array append: single append worst O(n) due to resize copy but sequence of n appends averages O(1) via geometric growth (double). Two, tight bound Theta vs loose upper O: stating O(n squared) for an O(n log n) algorithm is not wrong as a loose upper but Theta is the tight description — AXIS expects the tight one.

subsections.title: Growth chart that decides in 5 seconds
subsections.content: Constant 1, log n ~10 at 1000, sqrt ~32, linear 1000, n log n ~10k, n squared 1M, 2^n absurd at 1000. That stack predicts which beats which for given n without algebra.

subsections.title: Ignore constants plus lower terms illustration
subsections.content: 5 n squared + 1000 n + 100 behaves as Theta(n squared) because n squared dominates after some n0 — drop 1000 n and the 5 and the 100; compare growth shapes, not numbers for large n. Master theorem for divide-and-conquer relates fanout vs combine cost as described.

quickRevision: Big-O upper vs Omega lower vs Theta tight; drop constants plus lower terms; loose upper may hold but tight is Theta.
Growth: O(1) < log < sqrt < n < n log n < n^2 < n^3 < 2^n < n! — ladder plus ladder for fixed n=1000: log~10, sqrt~32, linear1k, n log n~10k, n^2 1M.
Best vs average vs worst via input: linear best 1, binary best 1 vs log worst, quick pivot decides best balanced vs worst quadratic.
Space vs recursion plus time: O(1) in-place vs O(n) buffer vs O(log n) stack; Master fanout vs combine via a vs b^d for divide plus conquer.
Amortized vs worst: dynamic array append amortized O(1) despite worst O(n) via resize copy; Theta is tight description, O is loose upper.
tricks: Any answer that uses best instead of worst for worst-case wording is swapping — worst must assume adversary input that maximizes steps.
Do not attach O(log n) worst to linear scan — O(log n) is binary via sorted; linear is O(n) worst.
Quick worst O(n log n) claim without remark on pivot is the favourite wrong — worst is O(n^2) with persistently bad pivot.
patterns: 'Upper vs tight?' -> Big-O upper vs Theta tight; drop constants plus lower terms.
'Growth versus for 1000?' -> Log vs sqrt vs linear vs n log n vs squared vs exponential plus factorial via ladder.
'Best vs average vs worst vary by input?' -> Linear first vs last vs target; quick balanced vs worst pivot; binary first mid vs last.
'Master fanout vs combine cost for divide plus conquer?' -> Compare a vs b^d as text-described.
'Worst vs amortized plus space vs in-place?' -> Worst per operation vs amortized per sequence vs O(1) in-place vs O(n) buffer vs O(log n) stack.

pyqPatterns.approach: Upper vs tight with drops, ladder for growth, best vs worst per input, a vs b^d for divide plus conquer fanout vs combine.

formulas.title: Arrays and Strings plus Two Pointers plus Window plus Prefix

formula.text: Arr base+i*size O1 | Str immutable copy | 2ptr ends meet | Window [left,right] grow shrink | Prefix sum = prefix[r]-prefix[l-1]

formulas.whenToUse: Any array indexing plus string plus two-pointer vs window plus range-sum MCQ.
explanation: Array index math base plus i times size gives O(1) random; insert or delete middle O(n) shifts; append amortized O(1) via resize copy.
String immutable plus repeated plus copies O(n squared) vs builder O(n).
Two pointers start at opposite ends and meet via condition; sliding window keeps [left,right] growing right and shrinking left per invariant.
Prefix sums range sum O(1) after O(n) build: sum(l..r) = prefix[r]-prefix[l-1].
Sorted plus prefix vs window vs two pointers decide which pattern the stem wants.

example.prompt: Sum of subarray l..r quickly after one building pass over the array?
steps: Build prefix where prefix[i]=sum up to i in O(n).
Window vs prefix vs two pointers: range sum is prefix, not window.

formulas.memoryTip: Index math O1, String copy immut, Ends meet two pointers, Window grows right shrinks left, Prefix subtracts before l.
formulas.commonMistake: Middle insert O1 — it is O(n) shifts. Repeated concatenations via plus are O(n squared) on immutable strings.

formulas.title: Stacks and Queues plus Monotonic plus BFS vs DFS

formula.text: Stack LIFO push/pop/peek top | Queue FIFO enq/deq/front | Mono inc/dec | BFS queue vs DFS stack

formulas.whenToUse: Any LIFO vs FIFO plus expression plus BFS vs DFS plus next greater plus circular queue MCQ.
explanation: Stack Last-In First-Out via push plus pop plus peek top; queue First-In First-Out via enqueue plus dequeue plus front.
Stack drives DFS plus expressions plus undo plus brackets; queue drives BFS plus scheduling plus buffering.
Monotonic stack keeps increasing or decreasing to solve next greater, histogram, trapped rain via indices.
Circular queue via bounded array plus head plus tail plus size plus one wasted slot or flag separates empty vs full.
Two stacks simulate queue and two queues simulate stack via reversals — amortized O(1).

example.prompt: Level order of a tree plus next greater of an array — structures?
steps: Level order is BFS via queue.
Next greater is decreasing stack via indices.
Expression evaluation plus brackets via stack.
